articles.title: The Live-Action Cyberpunk 2077 Movie Won't Retrace the Game's Steps, CD Projekt Confirms
articles.summary: CD Projekt Red has finally spoken up about the live-action Cyberpunk 2077 movie. The company said it doesn’t want to do a 1:1 adaptation of the game, instead telling a new story within the same universe.
articles.body:
CD Projekt Red has finally spoken up about the live-action Cyberpunk 2077 movie . The company said it doesn’t want to do a 1:1 adaptation of the game, instead telling a new story within the same universe.

"At this point, we can only say that we definitely don't want to make a film adaptation of the game," co-CEO Michał Nowakowski told Polish outlet PAP Biznes , via GamesRadar . "We want to tell a story in the world of Cyberpunk, but it won't be a one-to-one translation of the game's story."

The Cyberpunk movie is being created in partnership with Parmount, now under the Skydance banner after the recent merger . The film will be produced by Lorenzo di Bonaventura, of live-action Transformers fame.

It’ll be interesting to see how far the movie strays from the game, which featured a freelance mercenary called V who put a mysterious computer chip in their brain and ended up haunted by the digital ghost of Keanu Reeves’ Johnny Silverhand. I’d personally love them to go back, get Reeves back in, and tell Silverhand’s story before he ended up stuck in a chip.

Of course, the Cyberpunk universe — created by tabletop RPG designer Mike Pondsmith — is wide enough to tell a range of original stories. It’s fertile soil for pulling at themes of identity, autonomy, and the self as a ship of theseus to be modified and reprinted.

It sounds like a similar approach the company took to anime. Cyberpunk: Edgerunners feels like a faithful multimedia project within the world CDPR created — featuring locations and characters from the game world — but it tells a fresh story about original characters in its dystopian posthuman hellscape.

The Studio Trigger-led anime series is back on Netflix this month when Cyberpunk: Edgerunners Season 2 launches on October 20. Check out the IGN interview with the creators of Edgerunners for the lowdown.

CD Projekt also recently announced that work has officially begun on Project Hadar , its first game in its own original universe. The company has previously only played in the worlds of others, with The Witcher based on novels and Cyberpunk based on a tabletop RPG.

Elsewhere in CD Project Land, The Witcher 3 just got a remaster on consoles and PC, which saw the iconic RPG get a makeover. There were some issues with the new visuals, particularly heavy bloom in The Witcher 3 remaster , but CDPR was on the case quickly. And of course, Cyberpunk 2 is in the works, although it feels years away.

Kirk McKeand is a Contributor on IGN News. Find him on Twitter @MckKirk

articles.title: I Never Played Ocarina of Time, But 2 Hours With the Remake Proves There’s So Much More to This Masterpiece Than Nostalgia
articles.summary: I never played Ocarina of Time, but 2 hours with the remake proves there’s so much more to this masterpiece than nostalgia.
articles.body:
No matter how much I wish it were the case, I’ll never know what it was like to have seen Jaws in the summer of 1975. Yet, I still get the joy of watching the film that changed blockbuster cinema forever 50 years later, whether that be on towering IMAX screens or wonderfully restored 4K blu-rays. The experience of being there when a film, game, or piece of music entered our culture and witnessing its impact firsthand can never be replicated, but through preservation, remasters, and remakes, new audiences get to uncover these treasures for themselves.

This is the case with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. My recent playtime with a demo of the Switch 2 remake felt like digital archaeology; the unearthing of a cultural artefact that informed so much of what came after it, while remaining a gleaming treasure in its own right. A link between one era of video games and another. A sacred text. At least, that’s how it felt to me. You see, I’ve never played the original.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Preview Screenshots

Well, that’s a tiny bit of a lie — I did briefly mess around in the opening hour or so of the 3DS port around a decade ago. I know, I should be subject to whatever form of medieval torture you deem appropriate. But the truth is, it’s one that simply passed me by, despite having played several Zeldas since — Tears of the Kingdom is a masterwork of open-world design in my eyes, even if Wind Waker still sits closest to my heart. I never owned a Nintendo 64, and likely got distracted by whatever was happening in my mid-20s, which made me put down Ocarina’s portable version. But now, finally, I’m ready to right my wrongs, and after playing two hours of the remake, I couldn’t be more excited to do so.

During my time with the 2026 version of Link’s most defining adventure, I got to play through Kokiri Forest, wander around Castle Town, and complete the Forest Temple. Even from this small sample size, I could see flashes of some of my favourite games within it, and the inspirational sparks it must have fired off into other game developers' minds in 1998. But most importantly, I had a ridiculously fun time with it. From just that short session, I can safely assure you that, if you’re like me and have also somehow let this piece of history slip through your fingers, there’s plenty here for newcomers to enjoy. When it launches in November, there will be little excuse to leave it unplayed.

“Anyone who makes 3D games who says they’ve not borrowed something from Mario or Zelda is lying — from the games on Nintendo 64, not necessarily the ones from today,” said Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser to the New York Times . It’s a point that’s hard to argue with, and one I wouldn’t dare contest — I think one of the minds behind GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 probably knows more about game design than I.

Nintendo having created something of a lending library for game design is something I could see most clearly in the Forest Temple. I enjoyed unpicking each of its knotted series of corridors and unpacking its hidden secrets, all wrapped in a spooky mansion setting. Every room is a puzzle, whether in the more traditional sense of moving heavy stone cubes around to unblock routes or navigating combat challenges that put your tool belt to the test.

Battles are never overly challenging but wonderfully engaging, with looming sword-and-shield-wielding skeletons reacting to your actions as you, in turn, have to counter theirs with a well-timed dodge or stun. When striking them down, you can see the basic structure that would go on to influence Batman Arkham’s brawls — one of the defining melee combat systems — in the way that fights carry the rhythm of enemies reading your movements and you, in turn, having to react with the correct rock-paper-scissors response.

Outside of scraps, the structure of the whole temple can’t help but conjure memories of Dark Souls' intertwining, shortcut-unlocking approach to level design. Every route loops back to its central chamber, in which four coloured flames need to be lit in order for the path to the boss to reveal itself. The construction of this area is masterfully done, clearly indicating what you have to achieve without ever holding your hand too much. That freedom of thought has always been prevalent in Zelda, all the way up to how Tears of the Kingdom brings out your most experimental thoughts with its building systems.

In Ocarina, breadcrumbs of clues as to how to achieve objectives are given, with tempting buttons placed out of reach behind locked gates and high up ledges seemingly unreachable. That’s until you realise you can rotate the hallways and alter the architecture of the temple completely, like some sort of prototype of Dishonored 2’s Clockwork Mansion. This mechanic is key to navigating the space, and where much of its challenge lies. Entire projects, such as Fez, have gone on to use a system like this to power a whole game. Here, it’s utilised for less than an hour. It’s a testament to the enduring inventiveness of Nintendo that these ideas still echo through gaming today.

I found great joy in the simplicity of the temple, but one that tickled my brain enough to never seem like child’s play. There’s a delicate balance when it comes to signposting without holding your hand, to the point where the temple delivered several “aha” moments over the course of my time exploring it. Some came naturally through decades of playing video games, like seeing a frozen target with a raging fire nearby, clearly indicating I needed to fire an arrow through the flames to melt it. But some did give me pause for thought, such as not realising I needed to use my bow to knock each of the temple’s four guardian sprites out of paintings in order to progress. Still, I tried it anyway, and lo and behold, it worked. It’s that sort of “let's see if this works” experimentation that I’ve always appreciated in Zelda, so it’s no surprise to see it pioneered here in the series first foray into 3D.

I was pleasantly surprised to see that the temple’s boss, Phantom Ganon, was also a puzzle, instead of a toe-to-toe fight. Some of my favourite bosses in all of gaming are enigmas to be solved rather than tests of reflexes, whether that be any of Shadow of the Colossus’ beasts or, perhaps more analogously here, Elden Ring’s Rennala. Brain over brawn is clearly Link’s preference too, with well-timed parries key to bringing down this foe once you work out which of the ones charging on horseback out of the paintings that surround you is real.

One of the more notable changes this remake introduces is a jump button. Link was grounded in the original Ocarina of Time, only able to hop over specific gaps dictated by his creators. It was a decision intended to create contrast between Nintendo’s two big series. “You had to press a button to jump when we first started making The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time,” explained Yoshiaki Koizumi, a designer on the original game and Nintendo’s current Senior Executive Officer and Direct host, in an Iwata Asks . “As we were making Super Mario 64, we were thinking about The Legend of Zelda the whole time, and started talking about decreasing the action element in The Legend of Zelda and increasing the puzzle elements.”

Modern Zelda, and modern adventure games in general, have tended to favour action over puzzles, so it’s somewhat natural that a jump has been introduced in the remake. It’s almost impossible not to think of Breath of the Wild, and its sequel, Tears of the Kingdom, when going back to any older Zelda now. This remake’s Link certainly controls similarly to how those most recent incarnations of Hyrule’s hero do. There’s a great sense of responsiveness to each of his actions, whether platforming or in combat, with the latter feeling very familiar. No great surprise really when, even 20 years later, Nintendo still utilised the same lock-on approach to duels. In fact, it was remarkable to me how second nature much of what I played in Ocarina of Time felt to me, considering I’d never explored the Forest Temple before. You can almost see through the code, one that has been comprehensively studied and iterated on by Nintendo, and practically every other game developer since.

Just as you can see the impact of Jaws rippling decades later in the likes of Jordan Peele's Nope or Takashi Yamazaki’s Godzilla Minus One, Ocarina of Time can be felt in both the most recent Zeldas and adventure games in general. Of course, part of me always knew this. But as much as I enjoy those fantastic recent films, it's still Spielberg's shark hunt that stands tallest to me. It's remarkable how enjoyable these pieces of history still are today. It's far too early for me to know whether I'll feel the same way about Ocarina, but I’d be lying if I said the fact that I'm considering that after just a couple of hours hasn’t surprised me a little. I know this is a modern interpretation, but part of me expected this remake to feel slightly archaic; this is a nearly 30-year-old collection of ideas, after all. I was wrong. It feels full of freshly conjured magic.

Of course, Nintendo isn’t without its own inspirations. I realise 3D games were appearing on consoles such as the PlayStation years prior to Link making his N64 debut, and you can see flashes of them here. Perhaps I’m making decades-old observations here, but I enjoyed the way its twisting hallways resemble the original Resident Evil’s Spencer Mansion, rebuilt for an audience that likes to laugh in the face of horror rather than be chilled by it. You can see developers learning how to create explorable open spaces through time, from Capcom’s 1996 mansion, through Nintendo’s 1998 temple, to Rockstar’s 2001 Liberty City. It’s somewhat serendipitous, then, that Rockstar’s latest world, GTA 6’s Leonida, arrives just days after the Ocarina of Time remake. Two games of wildly different scope, but equally monumental. Digital archaeology prefacing a new age altogether.

I know that this game won't ever hold as special a place in my heart as it does for the millions who grew up with it, but there's still more than enough to make up for that. Just from this small sampling, I can tell it's an impeccably designed adventure that left me hungry to devour the full thing. If you’ve somehow let it slip as I did, I wouldn’t miss out this time around.

I’d never played Ocarina of Time before, yet, strangely, having played everything that it has come to inspire after, there was a comforting sense of familiarity. Now, I can’t wait to get my hands back on it and savour every moment of it for myself when it is released on November 5.

Simon Cardy is a Senior Editor at IGN who can mainly be found skulking around open world games, indulging in Korean cinema, or despairing at the state of Tottenham Hotspur and the New York Jets. Follow him on Bluesky at @cardy.bsky.social .

articles.title: The Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 Takes the Best PC Gaming Handheld and Adds OLED
articles.body:
Last year, Asus and Xbox worked together to launch the Asus ROG Xbox Ally and Xbox Ally X , and the latter is still one of the best handheld gaming PCs on the market right now. Not only is is great at playing games, but even amid the RAMpocalypse, the Xbox Ally X hasn't gone up in price and will still cost the same $999 that it did back in October 2025.

While the Xbox Ally X is an incredible little device, its relatively small display has been outclassed by the likes of the Lenovo Legion Go 2 and MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ — even though they're much more expensive. But Asus took the 20th anniversary of ROG to update the Xbox Ally X with an OLED display, and it takes the handheld to a completely new level.

With a better display and a new chassis comes a higher $1,299 price tag, but if you have the cash, that extra $300 is absolutely worth it.

Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 – Hands-On Photos

The Xbox Ally X20 has a fancier looking chassis and a much nicer OLED display, but it's functionally the same handheld as the Ally X beneath the surface with no real difference in the specs. It's still rocking the AMD Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme, along with 24GB of RAM and a 1TB SSD. It shouldn't be too surprising that performance is largely the same, netting 42 fps in Cyberpunk 2077 at 1080p High settings with FSR set to Quality compared to 43 fps from the Xbox Ally X with the same settings.

In 3DMark, the performance also lines up. The Xbox Ally X20 gets 598 points in the Steel Nomad test, compared to 602 points from the original Xbox Ally X, which is within the margin of error. In Time Spy, the X20 gets 4,030 points, compared to 4,016 points from last year's model — also virtually the same performance.

Of course, because OLED displays are slightly more efficient than your standard LCD screen, the Xbox Ally X20's battery fares a bit better than its predecessor. Starting from 100% battery, I played Cyberpunk 2077 until the X20 died, and it lasted 2 hours and 43 minutes with all stock settings. That makes it the longest lasting handheld I've tested, beating out the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+'s 2 hours and 14 minutes, and the Xbox Ally X's 2 hours and 34 minutes. You're only getting an extra 10 minutes of battery life, so it's not exactly groundbreaking, but it is an improvement.

If you already have the Xbox Ally X, it's not worth upgrading to the X20 based on specs alone. But the star of the show is the improved OLED display.

While I still love the original Xbox Ally X, the display has always been a problem for me. In a lot of games, especially as time has gone on, I've found myself needing to squint at the screen in dark scenes to make out what's happening. Likewise, in games like Monster Hunter Rise (which I've unfortunately found myself recently obssessed with), the original Ally X's screen isn't great at making the bright colors pop off the screen as well as an OLED display can.

For a long time, that led me to daily driving the Lenovo Legion Go 2, which has its own problems. I have pretty small hands, and there are times where I struggle to stretch my thumb to hit all of the buttons. Plus, with all the dials and buttons built into the Joy-Con-like controllers on the Legion Go 2, it's easy to accidentally hit something and trick the game into thinking you're playing with a keyboard and mouse, even for just a second. But because the screen is so good, I would just power through, and it's become one of the default ways I play games in bed, whether it's something that's running locally on the Legion Go 2 or streaming through Moonlight.

After spending a few days with the Xbox Ally X20, I've shoved the Legion Go 2 back into storage. The X20's screen is smaller, but it's much easier to hold for long periods of time, which completely equalizes it for me. Plus, the crystal-clear display makes it easier to see whatever's on the screen, so having less real estate there doesn't make much of a difference.

While the new OLED display is the highlight, the Xbox Ally X20 also has a new, partially transparent chassis that's evocative of '90s gadget design. It does look great, even if I prefer the simple black aesthetic of the original. The menu buttons are all gold now, which is apparently the standard color of 'anniversary' or 'celebration' editions of tech products, and other buttons, like the volume rocker and all the standard controller inputs, are black.

What's more interesting is the D-pad. Asus worked in a transforming D-pad that you can pull out and rotate to transform it from a classically defined pad with four directional buttons to a concave version akin to what you'd find on the Xbox Elite controllers. A lot of controller makers do offer this choice, but it's usually handled by having a removable D-pad rather than one that can transform. If you do have a preference for one type of pad, you can set it that way, but really, I've just been fidgeting with it because of the satisfying clicking noise it makes whenever you pull it out and rotate it.

The sticks have also been updated from the standard sticks on the Xbox Ally X to new TMR sensors on the X20. Day to day, that difference hasn't been noticeable for me, but it does mean that they should last much longer without stick drift. That's super important in a device where, if the controller breaks, you can't easily swap out the controller or its parts without taking the whole thing apart.

Unfortunately, It's Still Running Windows

Just like any other handheld, what really holds the Xbox Ally X20 back from greatness is the software. Windows 11 is still a pain to use with a controller, and while the Xbox Full Screen Experience does mitigate many of the problems, there are still some definite issues.

In the few days I've spent with the Xbox Ally X20, I've run into one specific problem over and over again: If I try to swipe up on the display to go to another window, the controller will bug out. It acts as though the Xbox button is being held down, which means every button press is read as a shortcut, either opening the keyboard, pulling up the task manager, or some other silly behavior. It's bad enough when I'm trying to scroll through my library, but when I'm trying to pull up a guide in a browser and swap back and forth, it makes the X20 unusable until I reboot the thing.

To be fair, the original Xbox Ally X had problems with the Full Screen Experience when it launched, too. But that was when it was brand new, and none of the problems were as toxic to the experience as making the controller essentially non-functional. I've been able to get around these problems with the X20's UI by avoiding using the touchscreen as much as possible, but that's not something I should have to do with a $1,300 device, especially when it's essentially just a chassis and display upgrade.

This should be something that future updates should be able to fix, but in the meantime, I'd advise forgoing Windows and installing SteamOS or Bazzite, unless you really want to use it to play Game Pass games or Call of Duty.

Looking at what is essentially a PC version of the Nintendo Switch 2 and seeing a $1,299 price tag is going to turn some people off from the jump, but I'm still surprised that this handheld is as affordable as it is. The Xbox Ally X20 has nearly the same specs as the Lenovo Legion Go 2, except with 8GB less of RAM, but it costs $700 less at the time of writing.

It's not hard to look at other PC gaming hardware this year and imagine that Asus could have raised the price more, considering the much-improved display and the addition of TMR joysticks. Just look at the Steam Machine , which came in at $1,049, or even the 4-year-old Steam Deck , which Valve bumped up to $789 back in May. Compared to the Xbox Ally X20's Z2 Extreme, 24GB of RAM, and 1TB SSD, the Steam Deck's aging RDNA 2 GPU, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB SSD at nearly $800 doesn't seem like that great of a deal at all.

Crucially, Asus also isn't discontinuing the existing Xbox Ally X, which is still a $999 handheld despite the price increases that have hit pretty much every other tech product this year. I keep bracing myself for what feels like the inevitability that Asus is going to raise its prices, but that hasn't happened yet. Now Asus is launching a new version of the Xbox Ally X, but with an OLED panel and TMR sticks for $1,299. That upgrade could be a bit cheaper, but it's hard to think of a single handheld gaming PC with an OLED display that is a better value right now.
